MIT reports onboard flight control for a tiny robot that still needs external power

The journal announcement describes a flyer with a 244-milligram sensing and computing package, while a human still supplies high-level commands.

RobotsBeat ↗19 November 2026English editorial summary
StoryImages 1Videos 1

A publication milestone for ongoing research

MIT reported the work on November 18 alongside publication in Science Robotics, following a February preprint. The flapping-wing robot estimates motion and controls flight using onboard equipment, removing the need for an external motion-capture installation surrounding the experiment.

Making room for onboard control

Retuned artificial muscles driving the wings produce a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, supporting a 244-milligram electronics package. It combines a microcontroller, inertial sensing, optical flow and a time-of-flight sensor. Together they estimate orientation, lateral motion and height quickly enough to stabilize the aircraft.

Onboard control is not untethered autonomy

Demonstrations include hovering, point-to-point flight and landing on a sunflower, with high-level commands sent by a human using a joystick. Power remains external. Batteries and a camera for object recognition and obstacle avoidance are future work, so pollination and crop inspection remain prospective applications rather than available services.
